title: Where and when: postpositions
intro: Turkish has no prepositions. Words like **for**, **like**, **after** and **since** come after their noun, as postpositions (*edatlar*), and each one asks for a particular case. This unit sorts them by that case, then adds the place nouns of *masanın üstünde* (on the table) and two ways to say how long something has lasted: *üç yıldır* (for three years) and *2020'den beri* (since 2020).

sections.title: Gibi, için, kadar, ile: no case

blocks.text: Four postpositions take a noun as it is, with no case ending: *gibi* (like, as), *için* (for, [A1 unit 12](gp-icin)), *kadar* (as … as, [unit 8](gp-equative)) and *ile* (with, by, [A1 unit 12](gp-ile)): *bir çocuk gibi*, *annem için*, *Ali kadar*, *otobüs ile*.

**Pronouns are different.** The singular pronouns *ben, sen, o*, the plurals *biz* and *siz*, and the demonstratives *bu* and *şu* go into the genitive before them: *benim için*, *senin gibi*, *onun kadar*, *bizimle*, *bunun için*. *Kim* can do either: *kimin için* or *kim için*. *Onlar*, *bunlar* and plural nouns stay bare: *onlar için*, *bunlar gibi*, *çocuklar için*.
*İle* is usually written as a suffix, `-(y)lA`, which joins the genitive form of the pronoun: *benimle, seninle, onunla, bizimle, sizinle*, but *onlarla*.

items.en: This present is for you.
There's no friend like her.
That's why I was late.
Ali is as tired as you.
Can I come with you?
This cake is for the children.

blocks.text: *Ben gibi* and *sen için* are wrong: singular pronouns need the genitive, *benim gibi*, *senin için*. But not *onların için*: *onlar* stays bare, *onlar için*.
*Bunun için* and *onun için* also link sentences: **for this reason, that's why**. *Yoruldum, bunun için erken yattım* (I was tired, so I went to bed early).

sections.title: Göre, doğru, karşı: with the dative

blocks.text: A second group wants the dative `-(y)A` ([A1 unit 7](gp-dative)), and with pronouns the dative forms *bana, sana, ona, bize, size, onlara*.

head: Postposition
Meaning
Example
English
rows: Bana göre bu film çok güzel.
In my opinion this film is very good.
This house isn't right for us.
We went to the match despite the rain.

blocks.text: *Göre* gives an opinion or a source: *bana göre* (in my opinion), *sana göre* (in your opinion), *Ayşe'ye göre* (according to Ayşe), *haberlere göre* (according to the news). In a question it asks for an opinion: *Sana göre hangisi daha güzel?* (Which do you think is nicer?)

*Kadar* after the dative is **until** in time and **as far as** in space: *saat beşe kadar*, *köprüye kadar*. You met it in *-DAn … -(y)A kadar* ([A1 unit 7](gp-ablative)). *Doğru* is **towards** a place and **around, towards** a time: *eve doğru* (towards home), *akşama doğru* (towards evening).

*Karşı* means **facing** a place, **against** something (*gribe karşı bir ilaç*, a medicine against the flu) and **towards** a person: *Bana karşı çok kibar* (He is very polite to me). *Rağmen* goes after nouns here; after a verb it needs a form you will meet in [B2 unit 3](gp-masina-ragmen).

items.tr: Ayşe'ye göre bu otel çok pahalı.
items.seg: Ayşe'|y|e göre bu otel çok pahalı.
items.en: According to Ayşe, this hotel is very expensive.
I'm at the office until five.
It rained towards evening.
We went into the sea despite the cold.

items.tr: Bu yoldan köprüye kadar düz gidin.
items.seg: Bu yoldan köprü|y|e kadar düz gidin.
items.en: Go straight along this road as far as the bridge.

blocks.text: *Doğru* also means **true, right** ([A1 unit 4](a1-u04)). After a dative it means **towards**: *Bu doğru* (That's true), *eve doğru* (towards home).
*Kadar* has two lives: with the dative it is **until**, **as far as** (*akşama kadar*); with a bare noun or a genitive pronoun it is **as … as** (*Ali kadar*, *benim kadar*).

sections.title: Önce, sonra, beri: with the ablative

blocks.text: A third group takes the ablative `-DAn`: *önce* (before), *sonra* (after), *beri* (since), *dolayı* (because of), *başka* (apart from) and *itibaren* (from … on).

head: Postposition
Meaning
Example
English
rows: Wash your hands before the meal.
Let's go to the café after class.
I've been waiting since the morning.
The schools are closed because of the snow.
From tomorrow on, I'm going to exercise.

blocks.text: *Önce* and *sonra* also stand alone as adverbs (**earlier, later**) and follow time spans: *iki gün önce* (two days ago, [unit 1](gp-time-past)), *iki gün sonra* (two days later). After a noun in the ablative they mean **before** and **after**: *yemekten önce*, *dersten sonra*. Before or after an **action** needs other forms, which [B1 unit 7](gp-dikten-sonra) teaches; for now, use a noun: *yemekten sonra* (after the meal).

*Başka* is also the adjective **other, else** ([A1 unit 8](a1-u08)): *başka bir şey* (something else). After the ablative it means **apart from**. *Dolayı* and *itibaren* sound a little formal: you will meet them in news and notices more than in conversation.

items.en: We drink tea after the meal.
Let me call you before the meeting.
I've been ill since Monday.
Nobody knows apart from you.
There's no match because of the rain.
From tomorrow on, I'll run every morning.

blocks.text: English **since** wants the present perfect: **I have been ill since Monday**. Turkish keeps the present, *Pazartesiden beri hastayım*, as French does: je suis malade depuis lundi.
After a time span, *önce* means **ago** and needs no ablative: *iki gün önce*. After a noun in the ablative it means **before**: *yemekten önce*.

**On, under, in front of, behind** are nouns in Turkish: *üst* (top), *alt* (bottom, underside), *ön* (front), *arka* (back), *yan* (side), *iç* (inside), *dış* (outside), *ara* (space between) and *karşı* (opposite side). They work like any possessed noun ([A1 unit 10](gp-genitive-possessive)): the reference goes into the genitive, the place noun takes a possessive, then the n of [A1 unit 10](gp-pronominal-n) and a case ending.

blocks.label: Place nouns
lines: evin     önüne     to the front of the house
yatağın  altından  from under the bed

blocks.text: **The case gives the direction**: the locative for where something is, the dative for where it goes, the ablative for where it comes from.

head: Turkish
English
rows: The book is on the table.
Put the book on the table.
Take the book off the table.
The cat came out from under the bed.

blocks.text: **With pronouns**, the possessive does the work, so the pronoun is often dropped: *(benim) yanımda* (next to me; with me, on me), *(senin) önünde*, *(onun) arkasında*, *(bizim) aramızda* (between us). **Between two things**, only the second takes the genitive: *bankayla otelin arasında* (between the bank and the hotel).

items.en: The keys are on the table.
The cat is sleeping under the bed.
Let's meet in front of the cinema.
The pharmacy is next to the bank.
There's a park opposite the school.
I don't have any money on me.

blocks.text: The n before the case ending is not optional after the possessive: *üstünde*, *arkasında*, never *üstüde* or *arkasıda*.

For a simple **in**, the locative is enough: *Telefon çantada* (The phone is in the bag). *Çantanın içinde* stresses **inside**. You will also hear place nouns without the genitive, as in *kapı önünde* (at the door): that is the compound of [unit 10](gp-compound-indefinite).
French builds some of these on nouns too: au-dessus de, à côté de, en face de. Turkish does it for all of them.

To say how long something has been going on, add `-DIr` to the time span and keep the verb in the present: *Üç yıldır Türkçe öğreniyorum* (I've been learning Turkish for three years). The suffix follows four-way harmony, and its D becomes t after a voiceless consonant: *iki gündür, bir aydır, bir haftadır, iki saattir, uzun zamandır, yıllardır*.

blocks.label: Duration up to now
lines: time span + -DIr, verb in the present
üç yıldır, iki gündür, bir saattir

blocks.text: **Span or starting point.** `-DIr` measures a span; `-DAn beri`, from the last section, names the starting point. Both keep the present. To ask, say *Ne zamandır?* or *Ne zamandan beri?* (How long? Since when?): *Ne zamandır buradasın?* (How long have you been here?)

With a negative, the past is common: *Üç yıldır onu görmedim* (I haven't seen her for three years). For a period that is over, use the past and no `-DIr`: *Üç yıl Ankara'da oturdum* (I lived in Ankara for three years, and don't any more).

items.en: I've been learning Turkish for three years.
I've been waiting for you for two hours!
How long have you been in Istanbul?
It's been raining for a week.
We've been living in Ankara since 2020.
I haven't seen him for a long time.

blocks.text: This `-DIr` is not the formal **is** of [A1 unit 3](gp-copula-present) (*Doktordur*): it sits on a time span, and the sentence has a verb of its own.
*Üç yıldır Ankara'da oturuyorum* (I've lived in Ankara for three years: I still do) is not *Üç yıl Ankara'da oturdum* (I lived there for three years: it's over).
French uses the present too: j'apprends le turc depuis trois ans, *Üç yıldır Türkçe öğreniyorum*. English needs **have been**.

summary: *Gibi, için, kadar, ile* take bare nouns; *ben, sen, o, biz, siz, bu* go into the genitive (*benim için, senin gibi, bunun için*), but *onlar* stays bare.
*Göre, kadar* (until), *doğru, karşı, rağmen* take the dative: *bana göre, akşama kadar, eve doğru, denize karşı, yağmura rağmen*.
*Önce, sonra, beri, dolayı, başka, itibaren* take the ablative: *yemekten sonra, sabahtan beri, senden başka*.
Place nouns *üst, alt, ön, arka, yan, iç, dış, ara, karşı* follow a genitive and take a possessive, n and a case: *masanın üstünde*, *evin önüne*, *yatağın altından*.
With pronouns, the pronoun can go: *yanımda* (next to me, on me).
**For** a span up to now: time + `-DIr` and the present: *Üç yıldır burada oturuyorum*. **Since** a point: `-DAn beri`: *2020'den beri*.
A finished period takes the past and no `-DIr`: *Üç yıl Ankara'da oturdum*.
